facts.claim: "NRICH" is track 4 on Killer Mike's album MICHAEL, released June 16, 2023 on VLNS and Loma Vista Recordings. Its length is 4:40.
Cool & Dre produced "NRICH". Its writing credits list Render, Jones, Eryn Allen Koehn, Andre Lyon, Bruce Smith, Ricardo Valentine Jr. and Marcello Valenzano.
Rate Your Music's credits list 808-Ray as co-producer of "NRICH" and Rayshon Cobbs Jr as a writer. They also list 6LACK and Eryn Allen Kane as vocalists.
"NRICH" samples Pleasure's "Tune In" (1977) and The Last Poets' "Niggers Are Scared of Revolution" (1970).
Eryn Allen Kane sings the chorus of "NRICH", and 6LACK delivers a sung-rapped verse.

Killer Mike has said the MICHAEL sessions used the same core players throughout: Agape Jerry on guitar, Damien "Dammo" Farmer on bass and Warryn Campbell on organ. He said DJ Cutmaster Swiff of Outkast is on every cut. This is album-wide, not specific to "NRICH".
Killer Mike says Hannibal Buress introduced him to Eryn Allen Kane, who is featured all over MICHAEL.
The song deals with revolution and Black self-determination. It opens with the Last Poets sample, and Mike raps about the Greenwood banking company he co-founded.

AllMusic calls "Nrich" an empowering, Last Poets-sampling song. It places the track among church organs, choral vocals and booming beats on an album that draws on gospel, funk, soul and '90s Dirty South rap.
MICHAEL is Killer Mike's first solo studio album in 11 years, following 2012's R.A.P. Music. No I.D. executive produced it, and Mike began work on it in 2021.

research.lineage: The song sits in Southern hip-hop with a gospel and Dungeon Family/Three 6 Mafia-inflected sound, and it draws on Black-nationalist spoken-word through its Last Poets sample.

draft:
**NRICH** opens with a voice from 1970 cataloguing all the ways a people can shoot: off at the mouth, craps, dope into an arm, guns into the air on New Year's Eve. That's the Last Poets, from "Niggers Are Scared of Revolution," a spoken-word indictment that turns its anger inward. Killer Mike sets that list at the front of his song and spends four and a half minutes answering it, not with denial but with a plan.

The plan is money, and Mike means it literally. He name-checks Greenwood, the banking company he co-founded, and stacks the bars with ownership talk: "They used to own us, but now we own us, that's independence." It plays as a sermon, and AllMusic places it among the church organs and Dirty South booming of the album MICHAEL, his first solo record in 11 years. But the boasts carry a sore spot. He remembers clothes that made him "embarrassed," then moves "through the Louvre smooth" in Paris. He traces his start plainly, "Born at Grady, a bastard baby to single lady," and credits God with getting him out. Then comes the line that gives the rest away: "It's underwhelmin' to be so overly underrated." The pride is real, and so is the wound of not being seen. A spoken aside makes the bind explicit: they should be celebrated, but like everything else they'll have to fight for it. Mike doesn't settle that tension. He puts on the gloves.

Cool & Dre produced it, with 808-Ray co-producing, and they keep it clean and close. A low synth bass repeats a simple line under kick, dry snare and hi-hat. A high synth pad hangs above the beat, and the mid-tempo groove stays relaxed, never rushing the verses. The rapping sits dry and upfront, every syllable clear, and a harmonized vocal floats in against it. A 1977 Pleasure record, "Tune In," is folded into the sample bed, so the funk lineage runs right alongside the protest-poetry one.

The guests do different work. 6LACK half-sings his verse, all compact rhymes and street-level caution. Eryn Allen Kane, whom Hannibal Buress introduced to Mike, takes the chorus and turns the economics into a hymn: run up billions, build a village, walk by faith. Her refrain that time will reveal the truth lands like a benediction after Mike's ledger of grievances and gains.

The song holds the Last Poets' disappointment and Mike's ambition in the same room, and you leave carrying both: the hurt of a people told they're less, and the stubborn joy of someone who decided to own the answer.

factCheck.claim: NRICH opens with a voice from 1970 (the Last Poets, 'Niggers Are Scared of Revolution') cataloguing all the ways a people can shoot
factCheck.note: The packet supports that the song opens with the Last Poets sample (1970). It doesn't say the shooting list is the sample's content. Reworded so the sample and the lyric's opening lines are stated separately.

factCheck.claim: The Last Poets track is a spoken-word indictment that turns its anger inward
factCheck.note: Only the Black-nationalist spoken-word lineage is supported. 'Turns its anger inward' is unsupported and was removed.

factCheck.claim: list of shooting: off at the mouth, craps, dope into an arm, guns into the air on New Year's Eve
factCheck.note: The lyric says 'guns and rifles on New Years Eve'. 'Into the air' is not in the lyric and was removed.
